overview.text: The Life-Giving Spring is associated with a sanctuary of the Mother of God at Constantinople. The OCA remembers it on Bright Friday and separately notes an icon commemoration on April 4. These labels are retained without a guessed civil-calendar conversion.

blocks.text: The Museum of Russian Art’s description of the type places Mary above flowing water, surrounded by people seeking relief. Its exhibition distinguishes the central image from narrative scenes around the border. The displayed historical icon is one example of this subject.

blocks.text: The OCA recounts that, before becoming emperor, Leo met a thirsty blind man and heard instructions leading him to a spring. The narrative associates the man’s restored sight and Leo’s later accession with the Mother of God. Leo then built a church there. The source traces destruction and rebuilding after Constantinople’s fall, a new church consecrated in 1835, and further destruction in 1955.

blocks.text: In this published account, the name derives from the spring and the healings associated with it. The water, sanctuary, and intercession belong to one local sacred tradition. The museum description documents the visual arrangement; the OCA narrative supplies the church account of its history and veneration.
